case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
case.limits: Section 230 protects the republication of someone else's content. A generated sentence has no other author to point at, and courts have so far been unwilling to assume the answer.
case.holding: Section 230 bars treating an interactive computer service as the publisher of information provided by another, and notice of the content does not remove that protection.
case.why_ai_cites_it: The foundation of every argument that an AI provider is a conduit for material originating elsewhere. Whether a model output counts as information provided by another information content provider is the unresolved question underneath a growing share of AI defamation claims.

reading.body:
Zeran v. AOL is the foundation of every Section 230 defense an AI provider can raise, but whether it actually applies to model-generated output remains an open legal question with no settled answer.

The Fourth Circuit held in 1997 that an interactive computer service cannot be treated as the publisher of content provided by someone else, and that notice of harmful content does not strip that protection away. That holding made sense for a bulletin board carrying user posts, where another author existed to point at. The problem for AI is that a model-generated sentence has no separate information content provider behind it. The platform and the content originator are, in that situation, arguably the same entity.

Four live cases against Character Technologies are currently testing how courts will handle this gap. The data does not indicate how far any of them have progressed, what claims are at issue beyond the implied defamation context, or whether any court has yet issued a substantive ruling on the Section 230 question in an AI-specific posture. What it does establish is that Zeran remains the unavoidable starting point for any such argument, and that the AI industry's legal exposure on generative content is being litigated now rather than resolved.

section.name: AI Case Law: The Precedents Behind the Defenses
